title: Ireland’s earliest writing was carved up the edges of stones and read bottom to top

cover.alt: A weathered ogham stone with notches cut along its edge, set beneath a church window at Churchclara in Ireland.

body: Ogham is an alphabet of strokes and notches used mainly to write early Irish, and its earliest surviving inscriptions date from about the 4th century AD. Its original 20 letters, grouped in four sets of five, were cut along the natural edge of a standing stone and read from the bottom left upwards, then across the top and down the other side if the text was long. About 400 of these ‘orthodox’ inscriptions survive, most of them in Ireland and Wales, with others in Cornwall, Devon, the Isle of Man and Scotland. More than a third of the total stand in County Kerry alone.

Read upwards along the edge, the droim

slides.question: Out of 10 Irish ogham stones, how many are in County Cork or County Kerry?
slides.explanation: About 6 in 10: Cork and Kerry together hold 60% of Irish ogham stones, and Kerry alone has over a third of all known inscriptions.

left.label: Legend
left.text: Every ogham letter is named after a tree: the ‘Celtic tree alphabet’ of Robert Graves’s The White Goddess.

right.label: Scholarship
right.text: At most 8 of the 20 letter names are trees. The tree reading grew in the manuscript tradition around the 10th century.

slides.label: orthodox ogham inscriptions counted by Damian McManus in 1991
slides.text: Roughly 400 are known: most in Ireland and Wales, with Pembrokeshire holding the largest number outside Ireland.

slides.heading: Where it came from
slides.text: Nobody is sure who invented ogham. Most scholars think the Latin alphabet was the model; others point to runes or Greek. One theory sees a cipher made to hide Irish from Latin readers, another a creation of early Christian communities in Ireland, a third an origin among Irish settlers in 4th-century west Wales.

slides.question: How many letters did the original ogham alphabet have?
slides.explanation: Twenty, in four groups of five. Five extra letters, the forfeda, were added later, mainly in the manuscript tradition.
